title: Expression-bodied members (=> for methods and properties)
hook: When a method body is a single expression — like building a cache key from one string interpolation — C# lets you write it with => instead of wrapping it in braces.

blocks.text: Expression-bodied members use the => token to say "the entire body of this member is one expression." They work on methods, properties, constructors, indexers, operators, and finalizers. The compiler still emits a normal member — this is not a lambda delegate. It is just a shorter syntax when the logic fits on one line (or one switch expression).

entries.plainDefinition: A C# member whose body is a single expression written after => instead of a { } block.
entries.example: public string Key => $"user:{Id}"; is a get-only property with an expression body.

entries.plainDefinition: An anonymous function that can be assigned to a delegate type, like x => x * 2.
entries.example: list.Select(x => x.Name) passes a lambda; it is not the same as a method written with =>.

blocks.text: Expression-bodied members keep small, obvious APIs readable without ceremony. A Redis cache key builder, a one-line validator, or a switch expression that maps a string to an enum all benefit. Interviewers also use them to test whether you confuse => on a member with => in a lambda — they are different language features with different semantics.

blocks.title: When to prefer a block body
blocks.body: Switch to { } the moment you need multiple statements, local variables, or a local function. A one-liner that awaits, logs, and mutates state is harder to read than a short block — density is not a virtue when sequencing matters.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Count the expressions
items.body: One expression that returns or assigns a value? => is fine. Two or more statements? Use a block.

items.title: Check member kind
items.body: Methods, get-only properties, constructors (after the initializer list), indexers, and operators can all use =>.

items.title: Remember: no locals inside =>
items.body: You cannot declare a local function or variable inside an expression-bodied member. Extract a private method instead.

items.title: Mix accessor styles on properties
items.body: A property can use => for get and a block for set — common for lazy initialization with a backing field.

diagram.title: Expression-bodied member vs lambda
diagram.source:
flowchart LR
  A[=> on a member] --> B[Compiler emits a real method or property]
  C[=> in an argument] --> D[Compiler creates a delegate or expression tree]
  B --> E[Called as obj.Method]
  D --> F[Passed to Select, Where, etc.]

snippet.label: Cache keys as expression-bodied members
snippet.explanation: ForAttempt is an expression-bodied method — one interpolation, one return. SessionLock is an expression-bodied get-only property. The constructor uses => after : this(tenant) to run a guard expression as the constructor body.

snippet.label: Switch expression as a method body
snippet.explanation: The entire method is one switch expression after =>. Each arm returns an int. The discard (_) throws instead of inventing a TTL — a common interview trap is silently defaulting to zero.

snippet.label: Mixed get (expression) and set (block)
snippet.explanation: get uses => for a one-line null-coalescing fallback. set needs a block because it validates and trims — two statements. This mix is idiomatic and readable.

blocks.title: C# expression-bodied members vs JS class arrows
rows: Instance field holding an arrow function
Lexical this from construction site — can surprise you
Not automatic — must assign to Func<> explicitly
The field is already a function value

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Calling a one-line => method a "lambda" in an interview — it is a method with a shorthand body. Stuffing multiple statements into a ternary just to keep =>. Forgetting that expression-bodied constructors still run field initializers and : this(...) first. Hiding await plus side effects in a single expression body where sequencing is unclear.

interviewTakeaways: => on a member is a body form, not a delegate conversion.
Allowed on methods, properties, operators, constructors, indexers, and finalizers.
Local functions cannot be declared inside an expression-bodied member.
Prefer a block when sequencing or locals matter.
commonPitfalls: Calling a one-line => method a lambda in an interview.
Stuffing statements into a ternary to keep the expression body.
Forgetting that expression-bodied constructors still run initializers first.

jsTsCorrelations.note: class C { foo = () => this.x } creates a field holding an arrow function with lexical this. C# expression-bodied members are still real instance methods with normal this binding.
